holding_summary: In a summary proceeding to dispossess a tenant of a furnished house for nonpayment of rent, the court held that the statutory summary remedy applies to furnished lettings the same as to unfurnished ones. The tenant's argument that including furniture in the demise removed the case from the statute was rejected as an unwarranted narrow construction, and judgment was given for the landlord.

quotes.text: The conventional relation of landlord and tenant exists between the parties, an installment of rent is due, it has been duly demanded and remains unpaid, and yet the tenant’s counsel claims that, because furniture was included in the demise, the landlord is not entitled to the summary remedy furnished by the statute, but must resort to some other mode of obtaining redress. This objection is without warrant in law.
If this were not so the statute would have no application to furnished tenements, hotels, manufactories or saw-mills, because they contained furniture or steam power.
The landlord is entitled to judgment.

notes: Whether the landlord (a private owner vs. a commercial operator) is not established on the facts given, hence who_was_letting is unclear.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The court held that a lease's habendum clause limiting use of a leased camp-meeting cottage to 'a private residence' did not, absent express restrictive words, forbid the lessee from also keeping boarders and lodgers for hire there. However, because the lease bound the lessee to the association's constitution and reasonable by-laws, and those by-laws forbade keeping boarders or lodgers for hire without the association's consent, the lessee's practice violated the lease and was properly enjoined.

quotes.text: The referee has found that there is a framed house upon the lot which the defendant uses as a private residence for himself and his family during the entire year, and that he also keeps boarders and lodgers therein for hire, without the consent of the plaintiff and against its will.

We think, therefore, there is nothing in the habendum clause which should be held to restrain the defendant from doing what he is shown to have done, by way of keeping boarders and lodgers for hire at his residence.
the defendant in keeping boarders and lodgers for hire is violating a by-law enacted by the lessor which was binding upon the lessees and which the plaintiff has the right to enforce against him.
The result is that the judgment, so far as it grants an injunction should be affirmed and in all other respects, reversed.
